body:
The domain socket path is probably incorrectly specified to curl, as it is only shown with that `@` character in the netstat output. Maybe `-v` helps to figure that out.

Also, your specified URL doesn't look like a valid URL as it doesn't have two slashes after the `http:`.

I think the '@' sign is just a way netstat chose to denote it is in abstract socket namespace, because they begin with a NULL character which cannot be displayed.
Technically, perhaps the curl tool could support the same notation (and change to NULL).

After taking a closer look, I think libcurl option 'CURLOPT_UNIX_SOCKET_PATH' would also need some adjustments in order to work with abstract socket namespace, as otherwise it might consider the path parameter as an empty string.

Perhaps we can introduce a new 'CURLOPT_UNIX_ABSTRACT_SOCKET_PATH' which the app supplies without the null prefix, and the library adds it (and perhaps a companion --unix-abstract-socket flag for the curl tool would be more suitable than parsing the '@' sign).
@bagder The URL is correct without the '@' symbol when the server does not listen on an abstract socket.

> Perhaps we can introduce a new 'CURLOPT_UNIX_ABSTRACT_SOCKET_PATH`

We can do that, but we can also check for and parse a leading `@` character so that users can do exactly what @typeless did above. Or perhaps use an even more explicit markup that is less likely to ever occur in an actual file path.

This abstract path for unix domain sockets feature is Linux specific it seems.
@bagder Yes, this is a Linux specific feature.

I'm not sure how common is the 'netstat' way to denote abstract unix sockets ('@'), and as you mentioned, this might collide with an actual file name (admittedly, not likely). 
That's why I suggested the alternative tool option '--unix-abstract-socket' to match the suggested library option (which we could make only available on supporting platforms).

Meanwhile, I managed to reproduce this by using 'socat' tool to listen on a unix socket and to proxy the stream to a local TCP http server as below.

Regular unix domain socket:
socat UNIX-LISTEN:/tmp/foo.sock TCP:localhost:80

Abstract unix domain socket:
socat ABSTRACT-LISTEN:/tmp/foo.sock TCP:localhost:80

I've got curl to work with the abstract socket by making the changes at (draft): https://github.com/frenche/curl/commit/3e6f3f8fd113bcd11a59bdc22972eea70cd40847
Hmm, actually, the 'strace' tool also uses the '@' notation for abstract socket.

There is yet another problem to bear in mind.

The unix man page says that besides the first byte being a NULL to denote an abstract name, the NULL value has no special meaning in the reset of the name (and therefore the length must be specified).

This means that all the below examples are valid and distinct abstract names:
NULLa, NULLaNULL, NULLaNULLNULL, NULLaNULLb, NULLNULL

So to fully support abstract socket at the library level, we'll need the app to specify both buffer and len.
While for the curl tool, we might even need to encode the name in hex or base64.

HTH

Anyone checked what netstat and strace show for abstract paths that contain zero bytes?

It might make sense to for example support URL-encoding with %00 for zeros rather than having the entire thing as hex/base64.

For "\0/tmp/fo\0.sock" the strace tool gets it right:
bind(5, {sa_family=AF_UNIX, sun_path=@"/tmp/fo\0.sock"}, 16) = 0
But netstat only shows up to the second null (which doesn't work): @/tmp/fo

URL-encoded would indeed be simpler.
@typeless, @frenche feel free to submit a pull request for this for when the feature window opens again after November 2.

We can actually add an option named something like `CURLOPT_UNIX_SOCKET_PATH_ENCODED` and have that support a URL encoded path name and this should work fine to use an abstract name space path when prefixed with `%00`. Like `%00/tmp/test.sock` for the path in the original comment.

Alternatively we call it `CURLOPT_UNIX_ABSTRACT_SOCKET_PATH`, which also assumes URL encoding but always puts the initial zero byte in there so that `/tmp/test.sock` passed to this option would work.

@bagder I like the first idea, though perhaps CURLOPT_UNIX_SOCKET_URL would be more descriptive.

I'm trying to implement it, but came across another issue with unix socket. It looks like we don't distinguish between unix sockets and regular ones when reusing a connection and might reuse incorrectly IMO. I've also looked at the initial commit introducing unix domain sockets (https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/970c22f970f0172e6a4c98ccc3176c740ddaa1c6).

So I've tested it with the 'socat' command above:
socat UNIX-LISTEN:/tmp/foo.sock TCP:localhost:80
Then if I run:
curl -v --unix-socket /tmp/foo.sock http://abc/ --next http://abc/
I can see that the unix connection is reused, same happens with libcurl if set CURLOPT_UNIX_SOCKET_PATH to null or call curl_easy_reset() just before reusing the easy handle (it reuses the unix connection).

I've made a patch for this problem, which fixes my libcurl tests but not the '--next' example.
I think though, this should be fixed in the '--next' logic to have it invoke curl_easy_reset (judging by their manual pages, this should be ok).
My patch can be found at: https://github.com/frenche/curl/tree/unix_socket_reuse

Note, the fix is not complete yet as it lacks freeing of 'conn->unix_domain_socket' in the reuse_conn() call, but I'm thinking to refactor it so that reuse_conn() would not bother with freeing stuff but instead call conn_free() right afterwards.

Thoughts?

I think I found one more justification for the refactoring of reuse_conn() as suggested above.
The 'conn->oauth_bearer' is allocated in create_conn() before ConnectionExists(), but it is only freed in conn_free(), so it may leak if we decide to reuse another connection instead of the 'needle'.

issue.title: Don't mix unix domain sockets with regular ones

socket option matches.
